intro: The solo violin is tuned a whole tone high and made to sound like a rough country fiddle. Mahler gives it a lopsided dance, interrupted twice by a warmer Ländler; Death has borrowed the orchestra leader’s chair.

sections.label: A · A horn calls, a fiddle answers
sections.mNote: The solo violin’s strings are tuned a whole tone high

sections.label: B · Woodwinds dance in F major
sections.mNote: A gentler Ländler over held horns and plucked basses

sections.label: A′ · The fiddle returns with passion
sections.mNote: The strings tap with the wood of their bows

sections.label: B′ · The woodwind dance opens out
sections.mNote: The second trio takes a longer route through major keys

sections.label: A″ · The dance dwindles into muted strings
sections.mNote: Soft horns and harp surround the last quick figures

cues.title: A fiddle tuned high
cues.text: A horn calls and the solo violin answers, its strings tuned a whole tone above their usual pitch. Mahler asks for a fiddle-like sound, played forcefully. Muted viola and cello solos stir beneath it; the dance already feels slightly off balance.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, printed p. 275: horn opening, solo violin wie eine Fidel, muted solo viola and cello. The footnote requires a violin tuned a whole tone high. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Death takes the violin
cues.text: Bruno Walter supplies a name for this fiddler: “Freund Hein Strikes Up the Dance”. Freund Hein is Death, a familiar figure with an unsettling invitation. Walter passes on the title in a letter written at Mahler’s request in December 1901.
cues.evidence: Bruno Walter to Ludwig Schiedermair, 5 December 1901, written at Mahler’s request and quoted by Bettie Jo Basinger: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: A warmer dance in F
cues.text: The first trio turns to F major. Oboes and clarinets take over the dance, with held horn notes and plucked basses beneath them. The solo fiddle steps aside, and the woodwinds make the room feel much less crowded.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 280–283, rehearsal 3 onwards; woodwind trio over horns and pizzicato bass. F-major trio identified in Basinger’s guide: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A leaf for Arnold Rosé
cues.text: On 11 January 1902, the day before the Vienna performance, Mahler gives the violinist Arnold Rosé a manuscript leaf of this solo. In that draft the violin is tuned only a half-tone high; the printed score asks for a whole tone.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement describes the manuscript (solo violin “um einen halben Ton höher gestimmt”), given to Arnold Rosé the day before the Vienna premiere, with the final tuning a whole tone higher: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-2-in-gemachlicher-bewegung/ . The Vienna concert date, 12 January 1902, is on its history page: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-history/

cues.title: The trio dies away
cues.text: The first trio stays in F major to the end. Low strings murmur, horns hold soft stopped notes, and Mahler writes morendo as the dynamic sinks to pppp before the scherzo breaks in.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 283, rehearsal 4: morendo in the low strings, stopped horns and pppp: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fiddle grows passionate
cues.text: The scherzo returns in C minor. This time Mahler marks the solo violin leidenschaftlich — passionate. Other strings tap with the wood of their bows while a horn pushes its phrase into the foreground. The fiddler has plenty of company.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 284, rehearsal 5: Tempo I, solo violin leidenschaftlich, second violins col legno, first horn sehr hervortretend.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Böcklin’s fiddling skeleton
cues.text: Alma Mahler later claimed that Arnold Böcklin’s Self-Portrait with Death Fiddling (1872), in which a skeleton plays into the painter’s ear, inspired this scherzo. She and Mahler had not yet met when he wrote it; he did admire Böcklin.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger records Alma’s claim, the picture’s composition, Mahler’s fondness for Böcklin and the fact that the couple had not met: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation page reports Alma’s account: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-2-in-gemachlicher-bewegung/

cues.title: The second trio lingers
cues.text: The woodwinds recover the gentler dance, now with more room to wander. The trio stretches beyond its first appearance, letting its major-key phrases linger before the fiddle’s music can return.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the second trio’s enlarged form and lyrical digressions: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinets open into D major
cues.text: The trio reaches D major. Clarinets sing over harp arpeggios; the violins slide between notes while a contrabassoon reinforces the double basses. Mahler lets this country dance become extravagantly tender.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 295–297, the second trio’s D-major expansion, clarinet melody, violin portamento, harp and contrabassoon doubling the bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An afterthought for the basses
cues.text: The contrabassoon that doubles the double basses here was an afterthought. Mahler added it in the proofs, in bars 246–51; the plate had no room for another staff, so the published score labels one line “Ctrfag. u. Cb. unisono”.
cues.evidence: Paul Banks’s catalogue of the Fourth Symphony’s printed sources describes the proof revision in bars 246–51 and the engraver’s solution: http://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/Symph4/Symph4prints.htm

cues.title: The dance on tiptoe
cues.text: The opening tempo returns over plucked cellos and basses. Muted violins and violas run through their figures at ppp, while horns hold soft chords and piccolos pick out tiny ornaments. The same dance has become wonderfully light on its feet.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 299, rehearsal 13: Tempo I, muted strings sempre ppp, pizzicato cellos and basses, horn chords, harp and piccolos.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: F major takes over the dance
transitions.from: A · A horn calls, a fiddle answers
transitions.to: B · Woodwinds dance in F major
transitions.how: The C-minor scherzo gives way to the first trio in F major. A held oboe note and a playful clarinet figure emerge over horn harmony; the basses pluck the beat. Mahler eases the pace at Etwas gemächlicher, and the solo fiddle falls silent.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 280, rehearsal 3 and Etwas gemächlicher; F-major trio identified in https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: C minor brings back the fiddle
transitions.from: B · Woodwinds dance in F major
transitions.to: A′ · The fiddle returns with passion
transitions.how: The trio fades and the score restores Tempo I. Muted inner strings begin moving before the solo violin re-enters in C minor, now marked leidenschaftlich. A prominent horn and col legno second violins give the return a rougher edge.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 283–284, rehearsal 5 and the solo violin’s leidenschaftlich entry.

transitions.title: Trilling woodwinds recover the Ländler
transitions.from: A′ · The fiddle returns with passion
transitions.to: B′ · The woodwind dance opens out
transitions.how: The scherzo’s busy strings loosen their grip as the trio returns. Flutes and oboes trill over sustained horns and trumpets; harp and glockenspiel add bright touches. The familiar major-key dance now has more time to linger.
transitions.evidence: Full score, second trio, printed pp. 291–298; expanded trio described in https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: Muted strings recover the opening tempo
transitions.from: B′ · The woodwind dance opens out
transitions.to: A″ · The dance dwindles into muted strings
transitions.how: The enlarged trio slows and thins before Tempo I returns. Cellos and basses pluck beneath muted violin and viola figures marked ppp. Horns hold the harmony while harp and piccolos give the returning dance small, pointed accents.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 298–299, reaching rehearsal 13.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, II. In gemächlicher Bewegung, full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: Second movement, printed pp. 275–303, rehearsal figures 1–14: high-tuned solo violin, two woodwind trios and the muted closing dance.

timeline.note: A horn calls above soft woodwind trills; the high-tuned violin answers over muted viola and cello solos.
Violins, violas and basses gather around the fiddle in muted and pizzicato figures, with timpani and low winds.
Woodwinds lead the first trio over held horns and plucked basses; trills and harp add light.
Cellos and basses murmur beneath held horns as the trio dies away to pppp.
The scherzo returns: the solo violin plays passionately over horns, harp, bass drum and strings that tap col legno.
Muted trumpet, cymbals and timpani join the fiddle and the busy strings.
Muted horns and trumpets and a ringing glockenspiel punctuate the busy strings.
Flutes, piccolos and oboes trill above held brass notes; glockenspiel and harp brighten the second trio.
D major opens out: clarinets sing, violins slide, harp arpeggiates and the contrabassoon doubles the basses.
The trio swells and holds, with piccolo and flutes above divided strings, before the tempo begins to return.
Muted violins and violas play at ppp over plucked cellos and basses, with held horns, harp and piccolo.
Woodwind trills, triangle, harp and tam-tam glitter over muted strings.
Cellos slide on the C string over soft basses while the clarinets die away.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
